title: Parsing & formatting dates
objectives: Predict which instant `new Date(string)` builds from each ISO shape: date-only is UTC midnight, a date-time without an offset is local, `Z` or an offset is exact
Keep non-ISO strings (`"10/03/2026"`) away from `Date` parsing, parse a known format by hand, and read `<input type="date">` values as date-only strings
Format for people with `Intl.DateTimeFormat` (`dateStyle`/`timeStyle`, `timeZone`), and build machine strings with `toISOString()` or `formatToParts` instead of slicing localized output
Write relative times with `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat`, computing the value and unit yourself (`numeric: "auto"` gives "yesterday")

sources.title: MDN: Date — date time string format
ECMAScript spec: Date Time String Format
HTML spec: the date state (valueAsDate is midnight UTC)

questions.prompt: On a machine in New York, what does `new Date("2026-03-10").getDate()` return?

options.text: `NaN`: a date needs a time to parse

questions.explanation: A date-only ISO string is parsed as **UTC** midnight (the spec's rule, which MDN calls a historical error kept for web compatibility). Midnight UTC is 8 p.m. on March 9 in New York, and `getDate()` reads the local day. It's standardized, so every engine agrees. `"2026-03-10T00:00"` (a date-time with no offset) would have been local midnight, and `getDate()` would be 10.

questions.prompt: Which string names the same instant on every machine?
questions.explanation: Only the string with `Z` (or an explicit `+hh:mm` offset) pins the instant. A date-time without an offset is read as **local** time, so it means a different instant in every zone. The US-style and space-separated strings aren't in the standard format at all: how they parse is up to each engine.

questions.prompt: A CSV from a UK client contains `10/03/2026`, meaning 10 March. How should you read it?

options.text: Match `DD/MM/YYYY` with a regex and build `"2026-03-10"` from the captured numbers

questions.explanation: Non-ISO strings are implementation-defined, and V8 reads `10/03/2026` as October 3. `Date.parse` is the same parser. Formatting with `en-GB` afterwards only prints the wrong date in British order: once the parse guessed wrong, no formatter can recover the right one. You know the format, so parse it explicitly (and then check that the date exists).

questions.prompt: A German user picks 10 March 2026 in an `<input type="date">`, which displays `10.03.2026`. What is `input.value`?

options.text: A `Date` at local midnight on March 10

questions.explanation: The displayed format follows the browser's locale, but `value` is always normalized to `yyyy-mm-dd`: a date-only string, which is the right type for a date with no time. `value` is a string, never a `Date`. `valueAsDate` is the `Date`, set to midnight **UTC**, which is why `valueAsDate.getDate()` shows March 9 for users west of UTC.

questions.prompt: From an instant, you need a Tokyo user's calendar date as `YYYY-MM-DD`. Which code is right on any server?

options.text: `formatToParts` with `timeZone: "Asia/Tokyo"`, then join the `year`, `month` and `day` parts

questions.explanation: `formatToParts` gives you the date on Tokyo's wall clock as typed pieces, so the result doesn't depend on the server's zone or on locale punctuation. `toISOString()` is the **UTC** date, a day behind Tokyo for 9 hours of every day. Splitting localized output relies on a format MDN says may vary between implementations. The local getters read the server's zone, not Tokyo's.

questions.prompt: What does `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "medium", hour: "numeric" })` do?

options.text: Formats a medium date followed by the hour
Ignores `hour` and formats a medium date
Ignores `dateStyle` and formats only the hour

questions.explanation: The style presets (`dateStyle`, `timeStyle`) and the individual parts (`hour`, `month`, …) are two different ways to describe the output, and ECMA-402 throws a `TypeError` if you mix them. Use `dateStyle` + `timeStyle` together, or list every part you want.

questions.prompt: `new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat("en", { numeric: "auto" }).format(-1, "day")` returns what, and where does the `-1` come from?

options.text: `"yesterday"`; your code computed `-1` and chose `"day"`, because the formatter doesn't know the time
`"1 day ago"`; it compares the value with `Date.now()`
`"yesterday"`; it treats `-1` as a timestamp and compares it with today

questions.explanation: `RelativeTimeFormat` only formats a number with a unit; deciding that something was one day ago is your arithmetic. `numeric: "auto"` lets it use words like "yesterday" and "tomorrow"; with the default `numeric: "always"` the same call returns "1 day ago".

prompts.prompt: Send an instant in the one format every machine parses to the same moment.
prompts.explanation: `toISOString()` prints `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ`, always UTC with a `Z`, and any receiver parses it back to the same instant. (`JSON.stringify` would call `toJSON()` on the Date itself, which returns the same string, or `null` for an Invalid Date.)

prompts.prompt: Create one reusable formatter: a medium date and short time, on New York's wall clock.
prompts.explanation: `dateStyle` and `timeStyle` are presets the locale fills in; `timeZone` decides whose wall clock. Build the formatter once and reuse `fmt.format` for every row, instead of calling `toLocaleString` per row.

prompts.prompt: Pull the year out of formatted output without depending on the locale's order or punctuation.
prompts.explanation: `formatToParts` returns the same text as `format`, split into `{ type, value }` objects. Find parts by `type`; their order and the literals between them change with the locale.

prompts.prompt: Make the formatter say "yesterday" instead of "1 day ago".
prompts.explanation: `numeric: "auto"` allows phrases like "yesterday", "tomorrow" and "now"; the default, `"always"`, always uses a number ("1 day ago").

code: // The machine is in America/New_York (UTC−4 on March 10, 2026).
snippets.question: What are the three lines?
snippets.explanation: Date-only: UTC midnight. Date-time with no offset: **local** midnight, which in New York (daylight time since March 8) is 04:00 UTC. With `Z`: exactly UTC midnight. Two strings that look like "March 10 at midnight" are four hours apart, and on a machine in Tokyo the middle one would be `2026-03-09T15:00:00.000Z`.

snippets.question: What's logged?
snippets.explanation: The format allows any day from 01 to 31, so the string matches, and V8 builds day 30 of February: 2026 February has 28 days, so it rolls 2 days into March. There's no error and no `NaN`. MDN notes engines behave inconsistently here (some return Invalid Date), so never treat a successful parse as proof that a date exists.

snippets.question: What are the two lines?
snippets.explanation: `toISOString()` is always UTC, so slicing it gives the **UTC** calendar date: still March 10. In Tokyo it's already 08:30 on March 11. "Today's date" for a user is a question about their zone, which `formatToParts` with `timeZone` answers in a machine-readable shape.
